Hand: There is one scribe throughout. The hand is a large, clear, highly legible Gothic bookhand, well-spaced, with a set aspect. There is a close resemblance to textura quadrata, as the minims have distinct diamond-shaped feet, but there are also multiple features of bastard anglicana which make it difficult to designate a single script. The ascenders are particularly long, especially in the case of 'k' and the barred double 'l'; 'h' is often crossed with a bar, which does not necessarily indicate an abbreviation, and its limb consistently descends below the ruled line. Both long 's' and the 'st' ligature are used, the 'g' is closed with a separate horizontal stroke, and the 'y' has a long descender, which curves to the right. The closed double compartment 'a' is typical of the gothic script, whereas the 'w' is closer to the Anglicana form. There are consistent otiose strokes at the end of words, particularly following 'r', 's' and 't'. The spelling reflects the later date of the manuscript: 'th' replaces þ/thorn, which is retained only for the 'þat' abbreviation. The hand changes slightly in size and aspect through the manuscript. The text on f. 4r is notably smaller, for example, and on f. 47v, lines 6-10, the hand briefly becomes extremely pointed and angular, and uses bifurcated ascenders, two-shaped ‘r', and a capital 'a' composed of two curved strokes. Abbreviations: The scribe uses a number of common abbreviations throughout. ‘þ t' is used for 'þat', and 'wt' for 'with', most commonly in the forms 'wtin' and 'wtout'. Macrons are used to denote missing 'm' and 'n' in both the English main text and the Latin rubrics. A macron is also used twice on fol. 3v above 'both', to indicate a missing 'o'. In one instance (f. 47v), a barred 'p' is used to indicate 'er' in 'perfectly'. Punctuation: The scribe uses a punctus throughout, to indicate both the end of the sentence and caesura. The colon is also regularly used, along with virgulae, to mark caesura. Parentheses are occasionally used, as on ff. 62v and 64r. Corrections: All corrections are in the scribal hand and inserted superscript, with or without a caret mark. Examples of both kinds can be seen on f. 4v.

Volume I, containing Gildas and Nennius, from pages 1-40 has been written in one hand, of probable twelfth-century date. A different hand of the twelfth century has written Part III, containing Bede's De Temporum ratione, on pages 73-120. Part IV (122-194) containing Symeon of Durham, appears to have been written in the same twelfth-century hand as Part III. However, pages 191-194 contain matter written in several hands. The Life of Cuthbert from pages 195-202, together with the Old English Durham poem on page 202, have been written in the same hand. Miscellaneous different hands are responsible for the Visiones (217-220); Gilbertus Episcopus Lumicensis (237-242) and the miscellany of regnal lists (243-252).

Copied by a single hand in Anglicana formata, with choice and formation of some letterforms influenced by Secretary.The hand is clear and uniform with sparse linking between individual letters. The most common ligatures are: cr, th, ti, te, ht, st, ss, ge, ga, fu. The minims are formed by separate, vertical strokes, characteristic of Anglicana formata. Anglicana letterforms include a slightly truncated long r and 8-shaped g (but see below), w with bows, d with looped ascender, the initial and final position sigma-shaped s, the extension of the shaft of t above the head stroke; and closed v with looped left ascender. Secretary influence is visible in the consistent use of single compartment a, 2-shaped and short r and open-tailed g. Spikiness of lobes is not pronounced.

A total of fourteen medieval hands have been identified in the manuscript; thirteen of them use insular minuscule with variations between them with respect to the use of set or cursive forms. At least one, probably English, scribe contributed glosses in an Anglo-Caroline minuscule no later than the early eleventh century. The scribe of the main text, Núadu, names himself in a colophon on fol. 55r, Araut dinuadu. Since the form of his name is Irish, it has been suggested that he was an Irish monk working in a Welsh scriptorium.Seven of the thirteen Celtic scribes were first identified by Henry Bradshaw, who labeled them A–G, with A referring to Núadu. The remaining Celtic scribes were named ‘The First Revisor’, ‘The Second Revisor’, ‘The Matthus in Iudea scribe’, Cyfeilliog, ‘The Beginner’ and ‘“Antonius”, the Scribbler’ by Helen McKee. For further details on the scribes, see McKee 2000:9–31.

English vernacular minuscule. According to N.R. Ker, 'a neat, rather pointed hand: 'e' round-backed: long and low forms of 's' used indifferently: long ascenders and descenders: the ends of the descenders are usually seriffed.' The aspect is broad but pointed and slightly backward-leaning. Rustic capitals are used at the beginning of sections. Summary of the characteristics of the hand (from Takako Kato): Insular single compartment a is triangular, but rounded. The a component of æ is rounded triangular, and the same height as or slightly higher than e. Insular d is round-backed, with the short upstroke at 45º, and tapering backward to the right. e is round and its horizontal line goes up to the right and often finishes with a tongue. Insular f: the downstroke is straight with a wedged top and finishes with a serif that turns up to the right, and the tongue is longer than the shoulder. The shoulder consists of a upright diagonal and a short downward vertical line. Insular g has a flat top; the vertical stroke joins the horizontal bar towards the left, and the lower lobe is closed. The sizes of the upper and lower lobes are the same. Insular h: the ascender has a split top; both limbs are straight and have distinct serifs that turn up to the right at 45º. minims have distinct serifs that turn up to the right at 45º. r is insular. There are two kinds of s: insular s with a straight descender with a serif to the right, and a long s with a descender which descends slightly below the writing line. The descender of long s tapers slightly to the left at the end. t is round-backed and its head-stroke is horizontal. The back-stroke joins the head-stroke at the left side. The ascender of ð is tall at 45º and tapers slightly backward to the right. The prominent cross-bar has an upward serif to the right at its left end, and downward serif to the left at its right end. The ascender of þ is wedged or has a split, and its descender is short and has a serif to the right. The descender of ƿ is straight and finishes with an upward serif to the right. y is dotted and the first stroke is thick, whereas the second stroke is a thin line with a wedge of a split at the top, and its descender finishes with a upward serif to the right. ascenders are often split or wedged at the top (see b, l, þ). descenders: straight descenders are as long as the height of the body, or sometimes shorter, and often finish with distinct serifs that turn up to the right at 45º. (See insular low r, low s, ƿ). Abbreviations: the cross-bar of þæt has an upward serif to the right at its left-hand end, and a downward serif to the left at its right-hand end. macron has an upward serif to the right at its left-hand end, and a downward serif to the left at its right-hand end. the descender of ˥ is straight and usually has a serif to the right at the end. Its head slightly curves inwards. Sometimes a larger ˥ is used at the beginning of sentences. Punctuation: The punctus is used.

'As regards handwriting, Ll.1.18 at first gives the impression that it was the work of many hands, but (apart from very minor marginal additions) there were in fact only three: A, who wrote the bulk of the manuscript, probably over a period of time; B, who collaborated fleetingly with A early on, and who reappears to contribute a short later addition; and C, who appears in one quire only, a distinct booklet that A took into his compilation, and went on to use himself. Hand A's successive stints are often clearly discernible in frequent changes of pen or ink (or both), and his work shows signs of having been carried on intermittently, and probably in informal circumstances, as exemplars sporadically became available. The hands of all three scribes show variable mixtures of current anglicana and secretary features characteristic of the latter half of the fifteenth century, and both the duct and the selection of features in A's contributions were clearly affected by language, text type and the space available on the page.' Scribe A, Richard Fox, copied f. 1r (fragmentary table of contents), and ff. 194r-214v in a script with the overall appearance ofAnglicana (e.g. double-compartment 'a' and hour-glass shaped 'g'), but with a strong Secretary influence: note the regular use of an open 'w' (alongside the Anglicana 'w' that is closed by two bows); the consistent use of 'r' on the baseline, often 2-shaped, and the absence of the Anglicana long-r; and the lack of loops on ascenders. Also note the dominant 8-shaped 's' at the end of words, perhaps a stylized kidney-shaped Secretary 's', with the occasional occurence of Anglicana sigma-shaped 's'.

The manuscript has been copied in an anglicana script by the Franciscan friar John Holbeach [Holbeche] (fl. 1411) (see Origin for further details on Holbeach). It is possible, as Winston Black suggests (see the introduction to this catalogue record), that Holbeach added to a pre-existing combined herbal and lapidary on ff. 89-113). However, this is uncertain: the apparent differences between the handwriting in this part and the rest of the manuscript may have arisen from Holbeach's use of a darker ink and a quill with a broader nib, as well as an initial intention to imitate the style of the handwriting and decoration of his exemplar.

Further commentary on the scribal stints, arising from the 'Scriptorium' project (2006-2009): Hand A wrote Items 1-4; Item 6 (f. 16r only; remainder by a different hand); Items 7–32, 42-43. In Item 28, ff. 89r (lower half) to 92v and ff. 103r to 123v are in one of hand A's normal styles; ff. 82r–89r (upper half) and 94r–102v are probably by the same hand, writing to a smaller module, and selecting certain different letter-forms (notably 'g'). It is possible that different types of texts, and the switch from English to Latin, might have been an influence on A's ductus and choice of letter-forms. Consider, for instance, the final stage of Item 4 (f. 13v) and the following Item 5 on f. 14r. The Latin is slightly more spaciously layed out; we find an occasional alternative form of 'd' (straight rather than a looped ascender); however, this is clearly still the work of Hand A. Another example is the transition from Item 15 to 16: for the latter item A's writing speed increases, resulting in larger letter forms, the flattening of the minims of 'm' and 'n' almost to zigzag lines, and very open 'e'. Hand A here fits fewer words to the line, and fewer lines to the pages, suggesting that time was a factor in copying this text. The hunting cries in this section have been more carefully set out, and thus they visually stand out. Hand B is responsible for the continuation of Item 6 (ff. 16v-17r), and perhaps also for Item 33 (f. 130v). This hand shows a distinct looped 'g', a broken stroke in the bowl of 'd', and much less frequent use of backwards 'e'. Item 32 shows a similar formation of 'g' and word-final sigmoid 's'. Further contrasting letterforms between Hands A and B may be seen in the formation of Hand A's looped 'w' versus the near-straight strokes of Hand B's initial 'w'.Hand C wrote items 35-42. This hand is somewhat flatter in appearance and less carefully formed than Hand A. Hand C has a notable tendency to fill out the remainder of his line with a horizontal stroke. Finally, several other hands have added small items to the manuscript, such as Item 4 on f. 4v. The crossed-out section on f. 79v appears to be a later addition, though it shows some resemblance to Hand B's contribution on ff. 16v-17r. Even more minor notes and marginal glosses (for instance ff. 54r, 61r, 79r, 91v, 92r, 126r) may be the work of later readers or owners.

Minusucle h is particularly unusual, the ascender frequently does not meet the baseline, and the hook and the minim stroke for the 'leg' of the h frequently drops below the line or joins the next letter in an informal ligature. Annotations in the hand of (fl. c. 1290-1330). John of London was a major donor of manuscripts to St Augustine's Canterbury, and his annotations and sometimes his name appear in several volumes belonging to Canterbury that are not recorded as part of his original donation. Precise biographical details about John of London have not been been firmly established at the time of the composition of this record (2023), but John seems to have been active at Canterbury c. 1290-1330, and several plausible historical figures have been put forward for identification with his cognomen. A hierarchy of scripts was employed in order to differentiate between quotations from Boethius (typically also underlined in red) and the commentary across much of the text in this Part. However, the choice of scripts varies, and there is considerable fluctuation in the formality with which they are executed. Folios 3:2r-3:8v comprise textura quadrata for quotations and commentary, the latter executed in a smaller module, but drifting in places into Anglicana formata before returning to the more formal textura. Folio 3:9r begins similarly, however the commentary again drifts into Anglicana formata and the quotations likewise stray from strict textura, with the use of Anglicana letter-forms such as long r. Later, from around f. 3:21r onwards, the commentary becomes increasingly cursive, and although the script remains at heart Anglicana the influence of Secretary letter forms and the thick-thin contrast in pen-strokes becomes more apparent. From f. 3:39r onwards, the quotations themselves become fully cursive, too, with Anglicana formata adopted, before reverting to textura from f. 3:44r. Similar fluctuations between set and cursive scripts continue until f. 3:90v, whereupon there is a definite change in scribal hand, halfway down the first column of text. Quotations are at first written in Anglicana formata, but this is abandoned in short order, with both quotations and commentary written for the remainder in Secretary script.

On p. 488 there is a donation inscription in Latin and Old English recording the gift of the manuscript from Bishop Leofric to the religious community at Exeter Cathedral, his episcopal seat. The Old English portion of the inscription is in a later-eleventh century English Vernacular minuscule, and is in a hand of similar appearance to the hand that copied the Latin version of the donation inscription directly above the Old English text. ff. 1r-1v, 161r-202v, 251r-288v were copied by Hand A in a blocky mixed minuscule script, slanting slightly to the right, in pale brown ink, with consistent letter size.Syllabic abbreviations appear rarely and only at the end of lines, while superscript word endings are not in use. Breathings are angular and mute iota is absent. Use of the double dot is functional only, and there is accentuation of all lengths of nomina sacra. The double grave accent is in use. Circumflexes above breathings are sometimes expanded.The only punctuation used is the upper point. Headings for lections and cross-references are by the same hand, in Alexandrine majuscule script, in red ink. The heading for the eothina lections is written in epigraphic display majuscule in red ink.At the beginning of each quire copied by this hand, the scribe has placed a cross in the centre of the upper margin, using the same colour of ink as that used for copying the first text on the folio. A cross has also been placed on f. 266v, the last folio of Quire 34.

overview: hands: ff. 2r-56v, 203r-250v were copied by Hand B in an upright mixed minuscule script, in black ink. There is modest variation in letter size and occasional flourishing of tails into the lower margin, sometimes decorated with horizontal strokes. There are corrections by erasure.Syllabic abbreviations appear rarely and only at the end of lines, while superscript word endings are not in use. Breathings are angular and mute iota is usually absent but sometimes adscript. Use of the double dot is functional only, and there is accentuation of all lengths of nomina sacra, though they are often unaccentuated. Nomina sacra strokes are sometimes decorated with an X-shape. The double grave accent is in use. Circumflexes are small, even when placed above breathings. Headings for lections and cross-references are by the same hand, in Alexandrine majuscule script, in red ink.

The manuscript is written by the Belgian scholar , known as Levinus Ammonius (1485?-1556) (RGK I 10) in Greek and in Latin. Hand A: ff. 1r-41v, Hecuba, Orestes ll. 1-490.A mixed minuscule script, with variable slant, in brown ink, with modest variation in letter size. Letters are hanging from the ruling line.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings usually appear only at the end of lines, but occasionally elsewhere (e.g. common abbreviation of μεν). Breathings are curved and joined to accents; mute iota is absent. Accents are often joined to alpha, upsilon and omega. Alpha is drawn in two shapes: a rounded one and another one with a long oblique stroke; beta displays in bilobate shape; pi is in 'omega-like' shape, under a long horizontal stroke; tau is often high with an eyelet, especially when ligated to kappa; one of the two strokes of chi is prolonged in the lower left corner; psi is traced in the shape of a cross. The modern nu, small gamma, kappa, lambda and sigma telikon are present; the latter is angular and traced in four strokes.The epsilon-rho ligature appears in a distinctive form in which the upper part forms a closed loop.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, lower comma and full stop.

Hand B: ff. 30r-30v, 42r-118r, Hypothesis on Orestes, Orestes ll. 491-end, Phoenissae, and scholia.A mixed minuscule script, with very variable slant, in brown ink, with modest variation in letter size. Letters are mostly hanging from the ruling line. Hand B shows a more fluid and cursive tendency than Hand A.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings are rare and usually appear only at the end of lines. Breathings are curved and joined to accents; mute iota is absent. Gamma is high; theta is open, often with a little downward fluttering; enlarged lunate sigma is used often at the beginning of words; tau is high and with an eyelet; lambda is positioned low and often with long descenders; the modern nu and sigma telikon are present.Tails are occasionally flourished into the lower and outer margins. Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, lower comma and full stop.
Some Greek words occur in the text with Latin translation by a later hand (e.g. ff. 37r, 52r).

The manuscript was copied in a small upright mixed minuscule script, in brown ink, with consistent letter size.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear only at the end of lines. Breathings are angular and mute iota is absent or adscript, sometimes reduced in size. Use of the double dot is functional only. Nomina sacra are usually unaccentuated, but occasionally accentuated when more than three letters long, or with enclitics. Circumflexes sometimes appear above breathings, and can be somewhat enlarged when they do. Headings, hypotheses and chapter lists were copied by the same hand in Alexandrine majuscule script. In majuscule script (but not in the appearances of the majuscule form in the mixed minuscule), upsilon appears with a long, undulating tail.

The text was copied in brown ink in script combining elements of upright ogival majuscule and biblical majuscule scripts: both the narrow and wide forms of epsilon, theta, omicron and sigma are in regular use, while the forms of upsilon, chi andomega are typical of biblical majuscule, while other letters follow the ogival style. When appearing at the end of a line, omega often appears in a vertically squashed form.The horizontal stroke for nu is in use and there are some superscript word endings at the end of lines. Breathings and accents are in use.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, middle comma, question mark and full stop. Middle and upper points are occasionally marked in red ink, and on other occasions are very often accompanied by a cross in red ink. Headings and other rubric were written partly in the style of the main text but in smaller letters, in brown ink, and partly in a display majuscule script in red ink and gilded.

overview: hands: pp. 1-[470] Hand A: the text has been written in a minuscule script, vertical, hanging from the lines, calligraphic, belonging to the traditional type; letters tend to have a rectangular form; some are larger, such as kappa, majuscule delta, phi, csi, chi, theta. The script shows so-called pseudo-ligatures, in particular for the letter epsilon, in its majuscule form, whose central horizontal stroke stretches to the right and touches the base of the next letter; the lower edge of minuscule gamma tends to be placed to the left with respect to the vertical axis of the script. These features have been identified as characteristics of the style '' which has been linked with the area of Palestine and Cyprus, between the end of the 12th and the beginning of the 13th c. The script has, in particular, affinity to the epsilon à pseudo-ligatures basses rectangular stylisation of this type of script (see Canart 1981, pp. 46, 50-51; while Canart, based on the reproductions he had access to, was able to identify just one low pseudo-ligature in the script of the manuscript, for epsilon-ny, we are now able to say that others are present as well, as epsilon-omega, epsilon-pi, confirming his assumption that the script of GCC 403 belongs to this style). The text is written in black ink.

The main text was copied in an unusually large mixed minuscule script, slanting slightly to the right, with significant variation in letter size. The text of ff. 1r-3r was written in red ink, the remainder of the manuscript in brown ink.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear only at the end of lines. Breathings are usually round but sometimes angular. Mute iota is usually absent but occasionally present. It appears in a number of transitional forms, in adscript position but reduced in size to varying degrees (e.g. f. 50v, col. a, line 10, f. 65r, col. a, line 11) or below the right-hand end of the letter (e.g. f. 26r, col. a, line 10). Use of the double dot is functional only, and there is accentuation of all lengths of nomina sacra. Nomina sacra are occasionally uncontracted (e.g. f. 64v, col. b, line 12). Circumflexes are not expanded, even when appearing above breathings. Accents are sometimes joined to abbreviations. The double grave accent and marginal quotation marks are in use.Distinctive letter forms include minuscule delta with a very short ascender (e.g. f. 56v, col. b, lines 6, 11), majuscule lambda with the lower right-hand stroke curved inwards, majuscule lambda with the upper stroke elongated and coiled inwards (e.g. f. 72v, col. a, line 8), large lunate sigma wrapped around the following letter and extending further below than above, and large tau with the horizontal curved.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, lower and middle commas, question mark and full stop. Headings for lections on ff. 3r-18r were written in epigraphic display majuscule in red ink and gilded, and thereafter in Alexandrine majuscule script with some minuscule forms, written in red ink and gilded on ff. 20v-34r in red ink only on ff. 37r-83v, but with the reappearance of gilding on f. 85v, the last surviving folio with headings. Headings indicating the Gospel are written in the latter script, in red ink only on ff. 5r-20v, 26v and 37r-85v and with gilding on ff. 3r, 23v, 30v and 34r.

overview: hands: The manuscript is written in a mixed minuscule script, upright or slanting slightly to the right, in dark brown ink, hanging from the ruling line. Tau and gamma have hooked apices. The epsilon-xi ligature appears in a distinctive form in which the upper part forms a closed loop.Syllabic abbreviations and superscription usually appear only at the ends of lines, but occasionally in mid-line. Breathings are round and mute iota is adscript.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, middle and lower comma, and full stop.

The main text was copied by Hand B, in an upright mixed minuscule script, in brown ink. There is moderate variation in letter size, growing more dramatic towards the end of the manuscript. There are deletions by erasure.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear throughout the line. Breathings are both angular and round, and angular smooth breathings are sometimes used as apostrophes (e.g. f. 103r, lines 6, 11). Mute iota is subscript, or in a transitional position below and to the right of the letter. There is decorative use of the double dot, and accentuation of all nomina sacra. The double grave accent is in use.Distinctive letter-forms include minuscule epsilon with a pronounced curve at the top of the ascender, which is occasionally separate from the lower part of the letter (e.g. f. 93r, lines 9-11); zeta and xi with an undulating tail extending to the right (e.g. f. 3r, lines 10-13, f. 3r, lines 6-9); bulbous open rho (sometimes with inclusions of letters within it, mainly towards the end of the manuscript (e.g. f. 309r)); and an occasional omega with open spiralling loops (e.g. f. 309v, line 10). There are numerous ligatures with open-backed sigma.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, lower and middle commas, question mark and full stop. The question mark is occasionally used as a normal punctuation mark (e.g. f. 4r, lines 4-11).Chapter lists and notes of stichoi have been copied by the same hand in Alexandrine majuscule script.

The main text was copied in brown ink. The Latin text is written in Carolingian minuscule, the Greek in a western European majuscule script, without superscriptions of word endings or abbreviations apart from nomina sacra, which often appear in a longer form than usual, e.g. χρς instead of χς. Headings are written in the same style in red ink.The Greek text contains numerous spelling errors and corrections, while there are few in the Latin. There are deletions by expunctuation and erasure. Common spelling errors include confusion between eta and epsilon, reflecting non-native pronunciation.Diacritics are not used, apart from occasional acute accents, hooked at the upper end, and the occasional use of the double dot on iota and upsilon, not determined by function but appearing recurrently particular words such as ἵνα (e.g. f. 11r) and forms of ὑμεῖς (e.g. f. 12r).Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points. A large proportion of Greek words are followed by a middle point, probably to indicate word division. There are errors in word division. Some words appear with gaps within them, perhaps due to an erroneous word division, but joined with a curved line below, similar to a hyphen.

The main Greek text was copied in direct imitation of the early medieval western European majuscule script of the exemplar. In accordance with the exemplar, diacritics are largely absent, but the double dot often appears on iota upsilon, and accents of anomalous form occasionally appear, while the punctuation marks used are the lower and middle points.The Latin text, by the same hand, likewise imitates the form of the exemplar, in this case an Anglo-Saxon minuscule script.

The manuscript was copied in a calligraphic mixed minuscule script, slanting slightly to the right, in brown ink, with significant variation in letter size. There is frequent flourishing of tails into the margin, sometimes decorated with X-shapes, and frequent extension of final horizontals to fill a line, often decorated with a vertical stroke or X-shape. Vertical strokes also decorate some other letters and abbreviation marks.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear at the end of lines only. Breathings are round and mute iota is absent or in transitional forms, usually below and to the right of the preceding letter, but occasionally in adscript position but much reduced in size (e.g. f. 332r, line 2). It often takes the form of a dot rather than a line. There is occasional decorative use of the double dot, and accentuation of all nomina sacra. The double grave accent is in use. Circumflexes are often much enlarged and somewhat angular.Majuscule omega is often almost flat-bottomed, occasionally entirely so, and sometimes decorated with a vertical stroke (e.g. f. 329v, line 19).Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, lower and middle commas and full stop. Points are often accompanied by a second point in red ink. Headings were written in Alexandrine majuscule script in red ink and gilded.

The main text has been copied by Hand A in mixed minuscule script, upright or slanting very slightly to the left, in dark brown ink. There is only slight variation in letter size. Tails are occasionally flourished into the lower margin (e.g. f. 81v), and these are sometimes decorated with an X-shape (e.g. f. 50r). There are deletions by erasure (e.g. f. 120r, col. b, lines 10-11), and by expunctuation (e.g. f. 125r, col. b, line 18), which has on occasion been followed by an attempt at erasure (e.g. f. 143v, col. b, lines 23-24. Words omitted have sometimes been inserted by the scribe, in position (e.g. 119v, col. b, lines 8-9) or by the use of a reference mark (f. 143r, col. b, line 25).Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear only at the ends of lines, and extremely rarely, apart from the use of a horizontal stroke for nu. Breathings are angular and mute iota is in an early transitional form, in the adscript position but sometimes reduced in size. The double dot is used only functionally, and nomina sacra are accentuated only when more than three letters long or with enclitics.There are some irregularities in the use of breathings. In compound words where the main part of the word after the prefix begins with a vowel, breathings are sometimes placed on this (e.g. ἐἂν, f. 7v, col. a, line 6; ὅτἂν, f. 8r, col. b, line 19).The words or prefixes πρό and πρός generally appear with an upward diagonal stroke from the foot of the tail of the rho (e.g. f. 52r, col. a, line 23-col. b, line 1, f. 52r, col. b, lines 8-9 ). Majuscule lambda often appears in a distinctive form with the right-hand descender bent down parallel to the left-hand one (e.g. f. 10v, col. a, line 9).Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points and full stop. Headings for lections are by the same hand, in Alexandrine majuscule script, in red ink. The headings at the start of the synaxarion (f. 1r) and of the menologion (f. 141v) are by the same hand in epigraphic display majuscule, also in red ink.

The main text has been copied in an upright mixed minuscule script, in brown ink. There is only slight variation in letter size, apart from enlarged and flourished tau in the top line of text. Other letters occasionally have tails flourished into the margins, notably minuscule nu (e.g. f. 80v, col. a, lines 11, 13) and abbreviations of καὶ (e.g. f. 86r, col. b, line 14). There are deletions by erasure.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear only at the end of lines. Breathings are curved and mute iota is absent, with decorative use of the double dot and accentuation of all nomina sacra.There are significant irregularities in the use of breathings. In compound words where the main part of the word after the prefix begins with a vowel, breathings are often placed on this (e.g. ἐἂν, f. 92v, col. b, line 5; εἰσἐλθὼν, f. 130r, col. a, line 3). Other words sometimes appear with two breathings, smooth followed by rough, on the opening vowel or diphthong (e.g. ὦτα, f. 83v, col. b, line 1; ὑμῶν, f. 93r, col. a, line 16; οὖν, f. 146r, col. a, line 17), but this practice is not consistently applied. Diacritics are occasionally omitted, or smooth breathings used in place of rough ones. The scribe also made quite frequent spelling mistakes involving itacism and other confusions of sounds (e.g. ἔτη for ἔτι, f. 80v, col. b, line 16; σισμὸν for σεισμὸν f. 158v, col. b, line 2.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, middle and upper comma, and full stop. Normal middle and upper points are rare; instead, the scribe has usually placed two points in a horizontal line, which have subsequently been covered with a red cross, or a red vertical line forming a cross in combination with the flanking points. Headings for lections are by the same hand, in Alexandrine majuscule script, in brown ink. The heading for the start of the menologion (f. 171v) is written in epigraphic display majuscule, also in brown ink.

The text of the Gospels was written in brown ink by a single hand in an upright ogival majuscule script. The height of the letter omicron is about 2.5 mm. The rubricated title headings of the kephalaia were written in an upright Constantinopolitan majuscule script. The height of the letter omicron is about 5 mm. There is no descender on upsilon. The Greek text is written in a minuscule script by a practiced western scholar's hand, with persistent effort made towards aesthetic accuracy, and probably derived from printed models. The script is characterized by different capital forms, enlarged letters and marked oblique strokes, especially in delta.

Both Greek and Latin texts are written by the same western European hand. As the Latin one, the Greek handwriting is characterised by chiaroscuro effects. The Greek script is a minuscule; vertical and diagonal strokes tend to be rounded or sinuous, some forms are traced rigidly, and in general the ductus is slow. The handwriting can be dated to the 17th century. The text is written in brown ink. The scribe also wrote some scholia in the margins.

The manuscript is written in a mixed minuscule by a practised hand with claim to aesthetic effect, in black ink, with modest variation in letter size.In the main text syllabic abbreviations are mostly limited to καὶ and prepositions. Breathings are curved and mostly not joined to accents; circumflex accent is linear, the acute accent is inclined and slightly curved, similar to the circumflex, almost vertical the grave accent. The accent are often ligated to alpha, ypsilon and omega. Isolated trema is sometimes traced over iota and ypsilon; mute iota is present but not always used.The handwriting is characterized by an alpha traced in two strokes, a small beta in bilobate shape, high gamma and majuscule lambda lightly inclined and wide, with curved elongated stroke if ligated.Ligatures with alpha and lambda are traced from below, those with rho always with the preceding letter.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, lower comma and full stop. The same hand has added the rubrics and interlinear glosses in red ink, as well as the surrounding scholia in the same script but with greater use of syllabic abbreviations and superscript letter endings. The stroke over nomina sacra is sometimes decorated with an X shape. Accents are small, with only moderate expansion of the circumflex when it is placed over a breathing.Majuscule kappa appears with an elongated and hooked ascender. Zeta and xi appear with long, hooked tails.Punctuation used includes the lower, middle and upper points, lower comma, question mark and full stop. The same scribe has added marginal scholia in a small plain majuscule script with some minuscule letters, and headings in a larger version of the same script.

Considering the different manifestations of the script of this scribe (about them see Canart 2000), the script of the manuscript constitutes an example of one of the most exuberant manifestations of Basilikos' script, while it is upright, carefully traced, and it shows some forms of the traditional ancient minuscule, as for beta and ny. On ff. 35r-35v, a leaf that was probably added at a later stage, the script is traced with softer movements and does not show the ornamental flourished elements common in the rest of the manuscript, nor the pronounced contrasts in the letters' size; however, the presence of characteristic features of Basilikos' hand (for which, see Canart 2000, p. 177), such as, e.g., elongated zeta and xi, narrow theta, the big tachygraphic kaì, the flat epsilon-ypsilon ligature, sloping xi, loop delta-epsilon-sigma, confirms the identity of the hand. Variations in speed and accuracy are detectable within the leaves written in this hand, which seems occasionally very nervous (see e.g. f. 34r, ff. 55r-66r), but is sometimes also more vertical and accurate, see e.g. f. 27r, ff. 39r-41v).ff. 67r-113r. Hand B: the text on ff. 66v-118v is written in an archaizing minuscule, vertical, calligraphic, with reminiscences of the Hodegon minuscule in forms such as majuscule beta, zeta, and csi in ligature, round sigma. There are frequent inclusions and superpositions of letters. The same script is detectable on ff. 122r-207v of MS CUL Nn.3.14 (hand A). The scribe does not write regularly iota subscript. The ink is black. As in the case of Sabbas' script, also this hand shows a certain variation in the level of formality: while the script appears very accurately traced and uniform in forms and size in particular in the final part of the text of the Alexandra, and in the final part of the manuscript ( ff. 115r-118v), in the first leaves it is a little less regular (see e.g. ff. 66v-67v); the very first lines of f. 66v seems to be in Sabbas' hand. The variations in Sabbas' and hand B's script, and the coincidence of some forms allow to hypothesize an identity of hand A and B: Sabbas could possibly have been able to master two different types (and, in this case, levels) of script. Hand B shows sometimes forms which recur identical in Sabbas' script, such as the vertical ligature phi-rho (see respectively ff. 25r and 66v), epsilon-phi with epsilon reduced to a simple curl (see respectively ff. 43v and 103v), epsilon-omicron with epsilon reduced to a curl (see respectively ff. 41r and 105r), majuscule delta with a big 'hook' at the upper end (see respectively ff. 47v and 66v), 'tall' majuscule gamma, sometimes with ornamental 'hooks' at both ends (see respectively ff. 27r and 66v), minuscule delta with upright slanting to the left (see respectively ff. 45r and 70v), heart-shaped majuscule beta (see respectively ff. 23v, Sabbas' signature, and 70v). It was not uncommon for Greek scribes to be able to use different types of scripts. The contrastive use of scripts with a different level of formality, which is found in Byzantine manuscripts, was a way to enable the reader to distinguish easily text and commentary. The hypothesis needs more work, and a broader analysis of the question, in the light of the presence of both scripts of Sabbas and hand B also in MS Nn.3.14 (part II).

overview: hands: Hand A: The manuscript is written by Nikolaos (RGK I 327), as stated in the colophon, in an informal mixed minuscule script, below top line, upright in brown ink for the text and in red ink for titles. His minuscule follows the models of the typical scriptures of the Terra d'Otranto.The circular-shape letters and and elongated alphas are filled in red. There is a marked variation in letter size. Syllabic abbreviations and superscription are commonly used. Breathings are round and mute iota is absent. Nikolaos' informal hand is characterized by a fast execution with moderately sinuous and curved shapes. The tau is often high, with the horizontal stroke always curved and often elongated to the base, which sometimes leads to a hook shape (e.g. f. 30v lines 14 and 26).Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, middle and lower comma (rarely), and full stop. For further details on Nikolaos' script, see Jacob .Nicolas d'Oria Un copiste de Pouille au Saint-Sauveur de Messine (1985), pp. 139-143

Hand B: according to D. Harlfinger, the quire was probably written by the scribe and scholar (RGK I 18) in a Andronicus Callistus Andronicus Callistus, -1478 minuscule script. Breathings are curved and joined to accents; circumflex accent is hat-like; almost vertical acutes and graves. Isolated trema is sometimes traced over iota and ypsilon; mute iota is present but not constantly used.

Mondrain has identified the copyist of the manuscript as the Constantinopolitan physician, scribe and scholar active in the 15th century, in a slightly slanting and much ligatured Demetrios Angelos Angelos, Demetrios mixed minuscule practised scholar's hand.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript letter endings are often used and they do not appear only at the end of lines. : the four Gospels are written by the 15th-century Greek scholar and scribe (RGK I 61) in a Georgios Hermonymos Hermonymos, Georgios, active 15th century minuscule script in pale brown ink.Slanting slightly to the right, Hermonymos' hand shows cursive-like ductus without variation in letter size. The main text of the manuscript was copied by Georgios Moschos in a mixed minuscule script, slanting slightly to the right, in brown ink, with modest variation in letter size. Breathings are round and mute iota is absent or subscript. There is decorative use of the double dot. Horizontal strokes appear over names.The modern nu and sigma telikon are present. Large lunate sigma wrapped around the following letters appears in a distinctive form, with an elongated lower curve hooked sharply upwards at the end. Beta appears only in its long-bowed form, with the top loop smaller than the lower and often solid. The upper curve of minuscule delta is often dramatically extended, though this feature appears only in ff. 33r-163v.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, lower and middle commas and full stop.

The manuscript was copied in a mixed minuscule Perlschrift, slanting slightly to the right, in brown ink, with limited variation in letter size and some flourishing of tails into the lower margin, occasionally with ornamented tips (e.g. f. 116r). The same hand has added the headings, in Alexandrine majuscule script, in brown ink.Syllabic abbreviations are not in use, apart from the horizontal stroke for nu, which appears only at the end of lines, while superscript word endings are also not used. Breathings are both angular and round and mute iota is usually absent but occasionally adscript. Use of the double dot is functional only, and nomina sacra are rarely accentuated, and usually only when more than three letters long or with enclitics. The double grave accent is in use. Circumflexes very rarely appear above breathings. Nomina sacra strokes are often decorated with an X-shape. Marginal quotation marks of different types are used.Most majuscule forms are in use in the minuscule text, but not mu, upsilon or omega. The long-bowed beta is present, with a straight back and often angular loops.Punctuation used includes the lower, middle and upper points, lower comma, question mark and full stop. The lower comma is rarely used, small pauses being indicated mostly by the lower point.

ff. 1*v-2*v are copied in a Hodegon-style mixed minuscule script, with variable slant, in dark brown ink, with variation in letter size. Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word are not in use. Xi ligated to preceding letter is enlarged.Punctuation used includes the lower, middle and upper points, lower and middle commas and full stop.

The manuscript is written in a mixed minuscule script, upright or slanting slightly to the right, in dark brown ink, pending from the ruling line. There is only moderate variation in letter size. Ypsilon is majuscule and stigma is widely in use; syllabic abbreviations and superscription usually appear only at the ends of lines, but occasionally in mid-line. Breathings are round and mute iota is adscript without consistency.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, middle and lower comma, and full stop.

: The manuscript is written by the scribe Nikolaos (RGK I 330) in a Nikolaos minuscule vertical or slightly slanted to the right, with modest variation in letter size.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings usually appear only at the end of lines, but occasionally elsewhere. Breathings are curved and joined to accents; mute iota is present but not constantly used. Accents are often joined to alpha, upsilon and omega.Nikolaos' handwriting is characterized by the beta with long vertical stroke, pi in 'omega-like' shape, under a long and often curved horizontal stroke, rho straight or slightly curved to the left, and enlarged lunate sigma.The ligatures are frequently traced from below. Ligatures with rho are drawn up, traced in a single line and often with small closed loops.Punctuation includes the middle and upper point, lower comma and full stop.

Hand A: ff. 1r-129v A mixed minuscule script, vertical or slightly slanted to the right, in brown ink, with modest variation in letter size.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings usually appear only at the end of lines and rarely elsewhere (e.g. common abbreviation of μεν). Breathings are curved and not joined to accents; mute iota is absent. Accents are often joined to alpha, upsilon and omega. Alpha is drawn in two shapes: a rounded one and another one with a long oblique stroke; beta displays in bilobate shape; delta is triangular, with a small eyelet closed. Pi has a elongated horizontal stroke, and so also tau and theta, especially if at the beginning of the line. The modern nu, small gamma, eta, kappa, lambda and sigma telikon are presents.The epsilon-rho ligature appears in a distinctive form in which the upper part forms a closed loop. Tau-rho ligature is overlappingPunctuation used includes the middle and upper point, lower comma and full stop. Tails are rarely flourished into the lower margins, e.g. f. 127r.An identification with Manuel Tzycandyles (RGK I 255) has been proposed (see Hemmerdinger 1981).

Hand B: ff. 130r-210v.Hand B displays a mixed minuscule close the model of Hand A, but slanting slightly to the right, with denser text. There is an evident moderate variation in letter size. Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings are not limiteted to the end of lines.Breathings are curved, circumflex accent is normaly not link to vowels. Mute iota is absent.Tails are rarely flourished into the lower margins.

The manuscript was copied by Hand A in an upright Rossano-style mixed minuscule script, in brown ink, with modest variation in letter size. It has been assigned to a sub-type of the Rossano style, that of the omega paraphé (Marchetti, pp. 178-179; Lucà, 'Rossano', pp. 107-116; Julien Leroy, ). There are occasional deletions by strikethrough.L'oméga paraphé, particularité d'un scriptorium calabrais, Bisanzio e l'Italia: Raccolta di studi in memoria di Agostino Pertusi (Milan 1982), pp. 199-217Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear only at the end of lines. Breathings are angular and mute iota is adscript, but often reduced in size. The use of the double dot is functional only, and there is accentuation of all nomina sacra. The double grave accent is in use. Abbreviations and accents are sometimes enlarged at the end of lines. Marginal quotation marks are occasionally used.The flat-bottomed omega is present, and there are inclusions of letters within omicron. Distinctive letter-forms include majuscule alpha with an elongated diagonal, sometimes detached from the loop (e.g. f. 218v, col. a, line 6), ligatures with a horizontally elongated half-epsilon (f. 213v, col. 1, line 18), and frequent use of ligatures with a large tau inserted through the middle of omega (e.g. f. 69v, col. b, line 22). A horizontal stroke is placed over the word δύο (e.g. f. 112r, line 20).Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, question mark and full stop. The rubric has been provided by the same hand in Alexandrine majuscule script, in purple ink. Headings to the Gospels appear in epigraphic display majuscule, written in purple ink and gilded.Lucà and Spatharakis ( Corpus, p. 78) identify the same scribe as being responsible for Vatican City, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, MS Barb. gr. 482 and a manuscript now divided between Sinai, Monastery of St Catherine, MS gr. 234 and Saint Petersburg, Rossijskaya Nacional'naja biblioteka, MS gr. 297.

overview: hands: : the manuscript was copied by the Greek scholar and scribe Petros Hypselas (RGK I 349) (active between the end of 15th and the beginning of 16th century) in a scholarly-calligraphical Petros Hypselas Hypselas, Petros minuscule script in black ink.Slanting slightly to the right, Hypselas' hand shows cursive-like ductus without variation in letter size. Ligatures and abbreviations are rare, common and very clear. Beta is present in the bilobate and modern forms; tau and gamma are high, lambda is capitalized but small in size. The sigma telikon is present, the letters are often separated and easily recognizable, probably to facilitate reading by Western readers.Breathings are curved; accents do not join to letters or breathings, but the circumflex is traced in a single gesture together with the ypsilon or omega.

ff. 3-6, 8r-16v, 25r-104v, 113r-168v, 177r-347v, 415r-446v, 455r-502v, 504r-508v, 510r-510v: The original Latin text is written in half uncial script in brown ink, the Greek text by the same hand in Biblical majuscule script in brown ink, without accents or breathings. Mute iota is absent. There is non-functional use of the double dot. The horizontal stroke for nu is sometimes used at the end of lines. Punctuation in use includes the middle and upper points and two-dot colon. Various characteristics of this hand have been highlighted as indicating that the scribe was primarily trained in copying Latin. For instance, the article is often omitted, while the usage regarding Greek nomina sacra is archaic for the likely time of copying, whereas that for the Latin ones is more up to date. Letter-forms show possible traces of Latin influence, notably the resemblance of upsilon to a Latin Y. The dative forms ἡμῖν and ὑμῖν are consistently spelt incorrectly as ἡμεῖν and ὑμεῖν.

ff. 7*r-7*v, 169*r-175*v, 348*r-348*v: The Greek text of the replacement leaves is written in a majuscule script in black or dark brown ink, without accents and usually without breathings, but with occasional breathings in anomalous forms. Mute iota is absent. There is non-functional use of the double dot, which is sometimes incorrectly placed on diphthongs. Punctuation in use includes the lower, middle and upper points and middle comma. The Greek script is written by a scribe trained in Latin, and shows signs of Latin influence in the form of letters such as epsilon, kappa and upsilon, as well as displaying anomalous practices such as the form of breathings. Latin letters are occasionally used in error in place of Greek ones (e.g. f. 169*v, line 20, pαρρησια for παρρησια). There are frequent itacisms and other spelling errors, and the article is often omitted. The subscription to Mark and superscription to Acts on f. 348v are written in blue ink.

Breathings are curved and mute iota is not used non consistenly.The general appearance of the writing appears rigid, since the core of the letters is inscribable in a square and the strokes are often built at right angles (e.g. ypsilon), however the descending strokes are traced with some softness.The small majuscules beta, gamma, lambda and phi are present. : Andronikos Kallistos Andronicus Callistus, -1478 ff. 2r-290v.The manuscript is written by the scribe and scholar Andronikos Kallistos (RGK I 18) in a practised minuscule without any claim to aesthetic effect, related to the Druckminuskel.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript letter endings usually appear only at the end of lines and rarely elsewhere (e.g. common abbreviation of μεν). Breathings are curved and joined to accents; circumflex accent is hat-like; almost vertical acutes and graves. Isolated trema is sometimes traced over iota and ypsilon; mute iota is present but not consisitently used. Horizontal bars over names are extended.Kallistos' handwriting is characterized by the beta in bilobate shape, high gamma and lambda with curved elongated stroke if ligated, and enlarged lunate sigma.Ligatures with rho are drawn up, traced in a single line and often with small closed loops.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper point, lower comma and full stop. Corrections and additions in brown pale ink in the margins are by the same hand. This hand was previously identified with that of George the Cretan.

The overtext was copied by Neilos (Hand B) in a mixed minuscule script with variable slant, in black ink. There is significant variation in letter size, and frequent flourishing of tails into the margin. There are deletions by erasure.Syllabic abbreviations and superscript word endings appear only at the end of lines, except in the top line of a page or lection. Breathings are round and mute iota is adscript, absent, or in a transitional form positioned below and the right of the preceding letter. Occasionally it appears within a preceding omega (e.g. f. 45r, line 35, f. 109r, line 1). There is decorative use of the double dot and accentuation of all lengths of nomina sacra. Nomina sacra may appear unabbreviated when used in a non-religious sense (e.g. f. 39r, line 21, κύριος). Accents are sometimes joined to letters. The double grave accent is in use.There are inclusions of letters within omicron, and the ligature of sigma-upsilon-nu linked over the top is in use (e.g. f. 31v, line 36. Distinctive letter-forms include rho with its tail sharply swept to the right (e.g. f. 34v, line 15), minuscule zeta with a sharp corner in the upper left curve (e.g. f. 3v, lines 3-4, 6, 8), majuscule kappa with a flourished downward diagonal (e.g. f. 7r, line 6) and enlarged tau with the horizontal extended to the left and terminating with a blob (e.g. f. 8v, lines 2, 4-6).Punctuation used includes the lower, middle and upper points, lower and middle commas, question mark and full stop. The teleia of the ekphonetic notation (the red cross marking the end of a sense-passage) is often used also as a punctuation mark. A punctuation mark appearing at the end of the text on a page often appears as a more ornate cross.Headings are by the same hand, in Alexandrine majuscule script with occasional minuscule forms, in red ink. Some of the headings at the beginning of major sections are in epigraphic display majuscule, also in red ink. From the cross in the lower margin of f. 68v there is a change of red ink.

The manuscript was copied in a mixed minuscule Perlschrift, slanting slightly to the right, in brown ink, with limited variation in letter size and some flourishing of tails into the lower margin. The same hand has added the headings, in Alexandrine majuscule script, in brown ink.Syllabic abbreviations are not in use, apart from the horizontal stroke for nu, which appears only at the end of lines, while superscript word endings are also not used. Breathings are both angular and round and mute iota is usually absent but occasionally adscript. Use of the double dot is functional only, and nomina sacra are rarely accentuated, and usually only when more than three letters long or with enclitics. The double grave accent is in use. Circumflexes very rarely appear above breathings. Nomina sacra strokes are often decorated with an X-shape. Marginal quotation marks of different types are used.Most majuscule forms are in use in the minuscule text, but not mu, upsilon or omega. The long-bowed beta is present, with a straight back and often angular loops.Punctuation used includes the lower, middle and upper points, lower comma, question mark and full stop. The lower comma is rarely used, small pauses being indicated mostly by the lower point.

The recto was copied by Hand A in a slanted ogival majuscule script in black ink, with breathings and accents, and flourishing of tails into the lower margin.The horizontal stroke for nu is present, joined with a downward stroke to the right. The verso was copied by Hand B in an upright St Neilos style mixed minuscule script, in brown ink. There is little variation in letter size, and slight flourishing of tails into the lower margin.Syllabic abbreviations are not used, apart from the horizontal stroke for nu,which can appear in mid-line, and there are no superscript word endings. Breathings are both angular and round, and mute iota is absent. Nomina sacra are accentuated only when more than three letters long. Nomina sacra strokes are ornamented with pairs of vertical bars. The double dot is only used erroneously, on diphthongs (verso, col. b, lines 29, 31). Circumflexes sometimes appear above breathings, but are not markedly enlarged.Majuscule forms of epsilon, kappa, lambda, pi and sigma are present.Punctuation used includes the lower, middle and upper points and lower comma.

The text was copied in a mixed minuscule Perlschrift with variable slant, in brown ink, with minimal variation in letter size.Syllabic abbreviations are not used, apart from the horizontal stroke for nu, which appears only at the end of lines, while superscript word endings do not appear, although suspensions of word endings are present. The text was copied in an upright low epsilon style mixed minuscule script in black ink. There is moderate variation in letter size, and slight flourishing of tails into the margin. There are frequent low epsilon ligatures.Punctuation used includes the middle and upper points, lower and middle commas and question mark. The end of sections is sometimes marked by an additional point in red ink. Headings are written in the same style, with greater use of majuscule forms, in red ink.

The main text was copied by Hand A in a mixed minuscule script, slanting slightly to the right, in brown ink. The text was copied in a minuscule script, in black-brownish ink. The script is slanting to the right and executed with rapidity. It has few ligatures, breathings are curved; accents do not join to letters or breathings, but the circumflex joins the ypsilon; the iota mutum is in use. Alpha's loop is open, beta is small and in a heart-shape, delta is wide and frequently ligated to a following iota in a single stroke (e.g. f. 3r line 2 ἰδιότης). Tau shows the curved shape with no horizontal stroke, usual from 16th century.

The text was copied in an upright mixed minuscule script, in black ink, slanting to the right and angular, executed with rapidity with moderate variation in letter size. Alpha often has an open eyelet, beta is bilobate with separated loops, the lower one stretched forward, gamma is present in majuscule form along with the minuscule one. Majuscule delta has an elongated and curved trait, epsilon is rendered with a rod if preceding gamma or chi. Theta is in both the open and closed forms, rho is open and traced in continuity with ypsilon The modern eta, modern nu and sigma telikon are present. Minuscule pi is written with an horizontal formed by a stroke curving upwards from the left-hand loop and connected to it by a vertical line. Psi has a cross-shape. The sigma telikon is present and so is iota mutum, though without consistency. Breathings are curved; accents do not join to letters or breathings.This script has various similarities to that of the manuscript Cambridge, Christ's College, MS Rouse 263.

ff. 1r-8v l. 18, 9r ll. 16-19, 10r l. 4-10v lin. 6, 11v ll. 18-19 Hand A: a script datable to the 17th c., an informal small minuscule, slightly slanting to the right, characterized by ornamental hooks at the end of uprights.

The text was copied in a minuscule script, in black ink, with initials and numerals in red ink by the same hand. The script is slanting to the right and executed with precision. It has few ligatures, for example the overlapping of omicron-ypsilon for the diphthong and the small stirrup-shaped rho-omicron ligature. Breathings are curved; accents do not join to letters or breathings; the iota mutum is in use. Beta is bilobate, with distant eyelets, lambda is wide and developed below the writing line, xi is not very evident and almost a vertical line, pi has the closed shape, the descending stroke of rho has a small hook to the left, tau is curved.
